gaps.construct: p *int64 kept by the flag package and written later during Parse, while the caller reads the same variable
gaps.description: editable lends exclusive access for the length of one call; there is no long-lived shared reference, so 'shared Reference to an Int64' is invented. The whole flag package design (flag.Int64Var(&cfg.port, ...)) depends on this aliasing.
No dereference; 'set target of p to val' is invented.

gaps.construct: (*int64Value)(p): reinterpret a pointer to int64 as a pointer to the named type int64Value
gaps.description: No newtype, type alias or pointer conversion; written as a constructor wrapping the reference, which only works because Int64Value was declared as that wrapper.

gaps.construct: int64Value exists so the same memory satisfies the flag.Value interface (Set, String)
gaps.description: The point of the conversion is to attach methods to an existing int64; without interfaces or methods the purpose of the function cannot be expressed, only its two statements.
The doc names Int and Nat but no fixed-width types; Int64 is assumed as a refinement of Int.

doc_rules_contradicted: Changing an `editable` argument is not an effect, because ownership already says who can see it. (here the caller and the flag set both see p, so the write is a real shared-state effect with no uses line)
invented_syntax: type Int64Value is a reference to an Int64
given p is a shared Reference to an Int64
set target of p to val
notes: A four-line function, but it is the core of Go's 'bind a flag to my variable' idiom, which is aliasing by design. Scribe's ownership model (read, editable, consumed) has no way to say 'this operation keeps a reference you passed and will write it later'; a translation that returns the parsed value instead would be idiomatic Scribe but a different API. Configuration libraries in most languages use this pattern, so the gap will recur.
